name: Apollo 15’s third stage
intro: This crater was made by the third stage of the Saturn V that launched Apollo 15. The day before Falcon landed, the empty stage was steered into the Moon on 29 July 1971 to give the seismometers a test thump.

hotspots.title: The crater
hotspots.text: The stage made a crater 35 to 40 meters long, a bit uneven in shape. LRO’s cameras found it in their predicted area decades later.

source.label: LROC (LRO camera team): the Apollo S-IVB craters

hotspots.title: Coming in
hotspots.text: It hit at 2.58 km per second, about 62 degrees above the horizon.

source.label: NSSDCA: Apollo impact sites on the Moon

hotspots.title: Reading the shake
hotspots.text: The Apollo 12 and Apollo 14 seismometers recorded the crash. Scientists in Mission Control studied the readings to measure how vibrations travel through the Moon’s crust.

source.label: NSSDCA: Apollo impact sites on the Moon

photo.alt: People in an office lean over long paper charts covered in wavy lines.
photo.caption: Scientists in Mission Control study the seismometer reading from this crash.

hotspots.title: Scattered pieces
hotspots.text: Scout’s check: nothing is left whole. The stage shattered on impact and its fragments are scattered around the crater.

source.label: LROC (LRO camera team): the Apollo S-IVB craters

funFact: Scientists in Mission Control studied its seismometer signal on long paper charts.
whyLeft: Its fuel was spent after sending Apollo 15 to the Moon, so NASA used it one last time as a known seismic signal.
repurpose: It broke into pieces. Its scattered aluminium is a possible metal source for a future Moon base, if anyone can gather it.
